description: DELTA WATCH uses NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data to monitor geological and environmental changes across Egypt’s Nile Delta. It investigates land subsidence, coastal change, flooding, and soil conditions by comparing satellite observations over time. Interactive maps and visualizations turn complex data into clear insights, helping researchers and communities understand changing landscapes and potential risks to people, infrastructure, agriculture, and natural resources to support informed decisions.
summary:
Living in Egypt, I know how important the Nile Delta is to our communities, our agriculture, and our everyday lives. But I also know that the land we depend on is facing environmental challenges that are not always easy to see, such as coastal erosion, land subsidence, and flooding.

As a Petroleum Geology student, I have always been curious about what happens beneath the surface of the Earth and how we can use science to understand the changes happening around us. I wanted to turn that curiosity into something useful, something connected to a real problem in my own country.

That idea became DELTA WATCH. We created an interactive platform that helps users search for and explore satellite data from sources such as Sentinel-1 and NASA’s NISAR mission, focusing on environmental challenges in the northeastern Nile Delta.

For me, this project is more than just a website. It is a way to connect what I learn with a real environmental challenge. Our goal is to make satellite data easier to access and understand, and hopefully help students, researchers, and decision-makers take a closer look at the changes affecting this important region.
details:
DELTA WATCH is a project I developed individually for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It started with a question that became increasingly important to me: How can I use satellite technology to better understand the environmental changes affecting my own country?

As someone living in Egypt and studying Petroleum Geology, I have always been interested in understanding the Earth, its surface, and the changes happening beneath it. The Nile Delta is one of Egypt's most valuable regions. It supports millions of people, agriculture, and important economic activities, yet it faces serious environmental challenges such as coastal erosion, land subsidence, flooding, and changing soil conditions. I wanted to create something connected to these real challenges rather than develop a project that was only theoretical.

This is how DELTA WATCH was born.

I developed an interactive web platform focused on the northeastern Nile Delta, particularly Port Said, Damietta, Lake Manzala, and Baltim. Its main purpose is to make satellite data easier to find, explore, and organize for environmental research.

The platform provides an interactive map and a Satellite Data Search section that helps users explore available satellite records from sources such as Sentinel-1 and NASA's NISAR mission through services including the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF), NASA Earthdata, and the Common Metadata Repository (CMR). Users can search for data related to selected locations, apply filters such as geographic area, date range, product type, and data maturity, and explore product information, identifiers, and available access links. Search results can also be exported as CSV files for further use.

I also included the ability to upload and explore supported user-provided files, such as CSV and GeoJSON, and display previously processed land subsidence measurements when suitable data is provided. This is important because I wanted the platform to be useful not only for discovering satellite data but also for organizing information that can support further scientific investigation.

I built the website using Python and Streamlit. I used Folium for interactive mapping, Pandas for organizing and processing tabular information, and asf_search for searching satellite data records. The project was developed using a regular computer and an internet connection, without specialized hardware. I also used GitHub to store the source code and Streamlit Community Cloud to publish the website online.

What makes DELTA WATCH creative is its regional focus and the way it brings different satellite data discovery steps into one accessible platform. Satellite information can be difficult to navigate, especially for students or beginners who do not have advanced experience in remote sensing. I wanted to make that first step easier by creating a platform that connects specific environmental concerns with relevant satellite data.

Since I developed the project individually, I had to consider several things myself: the environmental importance of the selected locations, the reliability and availability of satellite data, the needs of different users, the simplicity of the interface, and the technical limitations of the available tools. I also made sure not to present unverified measurements as scientific results or claim that the platform performs analyses that have not yet been implemented.

DELTA WATCH is currently a prototype focused on satellite data discovery, exploration, and organization. It does not yet automatically process raw SAR images or independently detect floods, coastal erosion, or land subsidence. These are important directions I hope to develop in the future.

My intended impact is to make satellite data more accessible to students, researchers, environmental organizations, and decision-makers. I hope the platform can support environmental education, encourage further research, and help people pay closer attention to the changes affecting the northeastern Nile Delta.

For me, this project is personal. I started with an interest in geology and a concern about the future of an important part of my country. Developing DELTA WATCH individually was challenging, especially while learning the technical tools along the way, but it taught me that even a first prototype can be a meaningful step toward connecting science, technology, and real-world problems.
